name: Algeria
summary_text: Algeria criminalises same-sex sexual activity under the Penal Code of 1966, Ordinance 66-156 of 8 June 1966. Article 338 punishes a homosexual act with 2 months to 2 years imprisonment and a fine of 500 to 2,000 Algerian dinars and applies to both male and female same-sex conduct. The United States Department of State 2023 human rights report describes the offence as undefined homosexual acts carrying 2 months to 2 years imprisonment plus fines. The United Kingdom Home Office country policy note of 26 July 2026 confirms the 1966 Code remains the operative framework, citing a Human Dignity Trust legal summary updated in June 2026.  Article 338 provides an aggravated penalty where one participant is below 18 years of age, with up to 3 years imprisonment and a 10,000 dinars fine for the older participant. Article 333 separately punishes outrage to public decency consisting of an act against nature with a person of the same sex with 6 months to 3 years imprisonment and a fine of 1,000 to 10,000 Algerian dinars.  Enforcement is documented. Non-governmental organisations report arrests within the LGBT+ community, with little information on the trans identity of those arrested. On 24 July 2020 police raided a private home in el-Kharoub, Constantine Province, and arrested 44 people, 9 women and 35 men, mostly university students, over an alleged gay wedding. On 3 September 2020 a court sentenced 2 to imprisonment and 42 to suspended terms, relying on decorations and gay appearance as evidence.  Algeria provides no statutory route for gender transition. Civil-status gender-marker changes are theoretically blocked, with no legal gender-recognition procedure available.  Algeria has no legal framework for gender-affirming healthcare. Medical and surgical gender-affirming care is prohibited. Articles 274 and 264 of the penal framework could be used against providers, producing de facto criminalisation of provision.  Detained LGBTQI+ persons have no specific legal protections. Prison authorities separate persons deemed vulnerable, but no distinct protection applies to LGBTQI+ detainees. Civil society organisations report compounded discrimination against LGBTQI+ persons. The law does not recognise or respect the civil rights of LGBTQ persons.  Same-sex partnership has no recognition. Most attempts at unofficial same-sex marriage are blocked by police, including a documented attempt in 2005.

name: Estonia
summary_text: Same-sex sexual activity is legal throughout Estonia for both men and women. It was re-legalized on 1 June 1992 after restoration of independence, the specific criminal provision was removed in 2001, the age of consent was equalized in 2002 at 14 and was raised in 2022 to 16 for all persons.  Same-sex couples can marry and jointly adopt. The marriage equality bill passed on 20 June 2023 by 55 to 34, was signed on 27 June by President Alar Karis and took effect on 1 January 2024, with the first marriage recorded on 2 January. Estonia is the first formerly Soviet-occupied state and the only Baltic country to legalize same-sex marriage. Opposition filed more than 700 amendments to block the bill and all failed. Registered cohabitation has been available since 1 January 2016 under the Registered Partnership Act passed by 40 to 38 and signed by President Toomas Hendrik Ilves.  Legal gender recognition has been available since 1992, with the first correction of name and gender on a birth certificate recorded on 6 April 1992 through a medical expert committee. The current framework rests on the Common Requirements for Medical Operations for Gender Reassignment in force since May 1999 and parts of the Vital Statistics Registration Act in force since January 2014, originating in a decree of 24 April 1997. The process remains medicalised and requires a psychiatric or mental-health diagnosis. Hormone therapy has not been mandatory since February 2022, genetic testing is not required, surgical intervention has not been required since April 1997 though it is permitted one year after the directive, and there is no forced sterilization. No nonbinary marker is recognized. Advocacy continues for recognition based on self-determination, and ministerial intent stated in May 2023 envisages change based on self-identification with correct markers for non-binary people.  Estonia approved a national LGBT+ equal-opportunities action plan in 2025, developed over about two years by the Equality Policies Department at the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications and approved by Economy Minister Erkki Keldo. It sets targets across education, healthcare, employment and legal-framework reform, with special attention to trans wellbeing. Its trans-relevant commitment is to update the legal framework to support protections for gender identity and expression. A December 2025 account records adoption of the plan to strengthen LGBTI equality across education, healthcare, employment and the legal system.  Employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited. Sexual orientation discrimination in employment was banned from 1 May 2004 through transposition of an EU directive and by the Equal Treatment Act in force on 1 January 2009, which covers employment but not goods and services. Gender identity discrimination is treated as implicitly prohibited in all areas through the Gender Equality Act since 1 May 2004, interpreted to extend to transgender and non-binary people and to cover less favourable treatment in connection with other circumstances related to gender and gender-based harassment. Sources differ on housing, with one recording protection for sexual orientation only and another recording workplace, housing and healthcare protections as including gender identity.  There are no hate-crime protections recorded as covering sexual orientation or gender identity in one dataset, and hate speech and hate crime legislation is recorded as not including gender identity in another. The Penal Code since 2006 prohibits public incitement to hatred based on sexual orientation, with paragraph 151 requiring danger to life, health or property. A June 2023 draft to explicitly ban hate speech passed first reading in September 2023. Advocacy continues for hate-speech and hate-crime laws. Conversion therapy is recorded as not banned. Bathroom access is recorded as protected. There is no censorship, and LGBTI organizations can register.  Official protection signals are consistent. The Foreign Minister publicly supported Tallinn Pride and missions flew rainbow flags. Estonia joined 16 EU states urging Hungary to revise its anti-LGBTI laws. Foreign embassies and international missions in Tallinn issued a joint declaration for Baltic Pride 2017 held in Tallinn on 6 to 9 July, affirming LGBTI rights as human rights. An LGBT+ Community Support Group was formed in the Riigikogu in May 2023, chaired by openly gay Eduard Odinets. Courts awarded damages in February 2017 for failure to adopt partnership implementing acts and ruled in May 2019 that Rakvere City Council’s 80 percent funding cut to the Festheart LGBTI festival was unlawful. After the homophobic assault at X-Baar on 11 June 2023, police arrested and charged serious breach of public order with possible deportation, as confirmed by Interior Minister Lauri Läänemets.  Violence risk remains documented. In the EU Fundamental Rights Agency 2024 country sheet, 62 percent avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner compared with 53 percent for the EU-27, 40 percent avoid certain locations for fear of assault compared with 29 percent, 38 percent are open about being LGBTIQ compared with 51 percent, and reported work discrimination at 12 percent was below the EU average of 19 percent. Participants in the 2007 pride were verbally and physically attacked and no parade was held until 2017. On 14 July 2023 a court sentenced a Russian-speaking man to 12 years for the 2022 murder in Tallinn of a Jamaican trans woman met in a Tallinn Old Town bar, who was stabbed more than 34 times while trying to flee. The court imposed a harsh sentence for severity and rejected a provocation claim, noting she had asked his friend to tell him she was transgender and whether he was comfortable with intercourse a second time.

sources.title: ILGA-Europe 2025 Rainbow Europe Index
sources.documents: Comparative LGBTQ rights legislation ranking; Estonia ranks 21st of 49 European countries, lower than Finland/Sweden but higher than other Baltics and UK.
sources.detail: No URL in excerpt; cited as "According to ILGA-Europe's 2025 Rainbow Europe Index, Estonia ranks 21st among 49 countries"

Advocacy continues for recognition based on self-determination, and ministerial intent stated in May 2023 envisages change based on self-identification with correct markers for non-binary people.  Estonia approved a national LGBT+ equal-opportunities action plan in 2025, developed over about two years by the Equality Policies Department at the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications and approved by Economy Minister Erkki Keldo. It sets targets across education, healthcare, employment and legal-framework reform, with special attention to trans wellbeing. Its trans-relevant commitment is to update the legal framework to support protections for gender identity and expression. A December 2025 account records adoption of the plan to strengthen LGBTI equality across education, healthcare, employment and the legal system.  Employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited. Sexual orientation discrimination in employment was banned from 1 May 2004 through transposition of an EU directive and by the Equal Treatment Act in force on 1 January 2009, which covers employment but not goods and services. Gender identity discrimination is treated as implicitly prohibited in all areas through the Gender Equality Act since 1 May 2004, interpreted to extend to transgender and non-binary people and to cover less favourable treatment in connection with other circumstances related to gender and gender-based harassment. Sources differ on housing, with one recording protection for sexual orientation only and another recording workplace, housing and healthcare protections as including gender identity.  There are no hate-crime protections recorded as covering sexual orientation or gender identity in one dataset, and hate speech and hate crime legislation is recorded as not including gender identity in another. The Penal Code since 2006 prohibits public incitement to hatred based on sexual orientation, with paragraph 151 requiring danger to life, health or property. A June 2023 draft to explicitly ban hate speech passed first reading in September 2023. Advocacy continues for hate-speech and hate-crime laws. Conversion therapy is recorded as not banned. Bathroom access is recorded as protected. There is no censorship, and LGBTI organizations can register.  Official protection signals are consistent. The Foreign Minister publicly supported Tallinn Pride and missions flew rainbow flags. Estonia joined 16 EU states urging Hungary to revise its anti-LGBTI laws. Foreign embassies and international missions in Tallinn issued a joint declaration for Baltic Pride 2017 held in Tallinn on 6 to 9 July, affirming LGBTI rights as human rights. An LGBT+ Community Support Group was formed in the Riigikogu in May 2023, chaired by openly gay Eduard Odinets. Courts awarded damages in February 2017 for failure to adopt partnership implementing acts and ruled in May 2019 that Rakvere City Council’s 80 percent funding cut to the Festheart LGBTI festival was unlawful. After the homophobic assault at X-Baar on 11 June 2023, police arrested and charged serious breach of public order with possible deportation, as confirmed by Interior Minister Lauri Läänemets.  Violence risk remains documented. In the EU Fundamental Rights Agency 2024 country sheet, 62 percent avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner compared with 53 percent for the EU-27, 40 percent avoid certain locations for fear of assault compared with 29 percent, 38 percent are open about being LGBTIQ compared with 51 percent, and reported work discrimination at 12 percent was below the EU average of 19 percent. Participants in the 2007 pride were verbally and physically attacked and no parade was held until 2017. On 14 July 2023 a court sentenced a Russian-speaking man to 12 years for the 2022 murder in Tallinn of a Jamaican trans woman met in a Tallinn Old Town bar, who was stabbed more than 34 times while trying to flee. The court imposed a harsh sentence for severity and rejected a provocation claim, noting she had asked his friend to tell him she was transgender and whether he was comfortable with intercourse a second time.
